newsitem.title: USA: U.S. and Cuba meet on migration accords.
newsitem.headline: U.S. and Cuba meet on migration accords.

text.p: The United States and Cuba started two days of talks Wednesday to review the progress of migration accords signed in recent years, U.S. officials said.

The talks on migration, one of the few areas in which Washington and Havana cooperate, started days after Cuba charged that people in the United States were behind the bombing of two hotels in Havana last weekend and withdrew its baseball team from a series against the United States in Connecticut.
The U.S. government said the charges were unsupported.

U.S. officials said the delegations meeting at the U.S. mission to the United Nations in New York would focus on technical matters related to the agreements of September 1994 and May 1995. The last such discussions took place in Havana last December.

Under the 1995 agreement, Washington undertook to repatriate Cuban boat people intercepted trying to reach the United States, while at the same time increasing the number of visas it grants Cubans to 20,000 a year.

The aim, largely achieved, was to halt a flow of Cuban boat people over the Florida Straits that reached crisis point in August 1994 when more than 30,000 Cubans left the communist-ruled island on flimsy rafts.
The two countries, which have no diplomatic relations, have been political enemies since the 1959 revolution that brought Cuban President Fidel Castro to power.

The U.S. delegation to the New York talks is led by John Hamilton, assistant secretary of state for Central American, Caribbean and Cuban affairs. Cuban parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon heads the Cuban side.
